title: What a retrieval pipeline is responsible for
text: Retrieval is not the same job as writing. A retrieval pipeline finds passages that can support an answer and leaves the wording to a later step. A production question-answering system embeds the user question, pulls a small set of chunks, and passes those chunks downstream as evidence. The writer should not see the whole corpus. Keeping retrieval separate makes it possible to measure precision before anyone reads the prose, and it gives a later check a concrete list of allowed sources. If the retriever returns nothing useful, the honest brief says the evidence is thin instead of filling the gap from model memory.

title: Hybrid search on a small corpus
text: Lexical overlap and vector similarity fail in different ways. A rare token such as a metric name is a strong keyword signal, while a hashing embedder can smear that same token across a fixed set of dimensions. Hybrid search adds a keyword score to a cosine score so a note that actually contains the question's terms outranks a note that is only vaguely near it. On a small local corpus this is enough to demonstrate retrieval without an API key. The same search function can later call a hosted embedder. Because the blend lives in code, changing one weight has a predictable effect on the ranking.

title: Precision at k, in plain language
text: Precision at k is the fraction of the top k retrieved items that are relevant. It does not reward a system for hiding a good document far down the list. Mean precision at k averages that fraction over a labeled query set. A worked example belongs in code, not in a model's head: take the binary judgments, cut each list at k, divide the number of relevant hits by k, then average across queries. Report the sample size next to the figure. A metric computed from three hand-labeled queries is a teaching example, not a leaderboard result.

title: When one prompt is not enough
text: A single prompt can draft a paragraph. It cannot show its retrieval, its arithmetic, or its decision to stop. An agentic workflow splits those jobs across roles: one step searches, one step runs code, one step writes, and one step reviews. The split is what makes a trace readable, and it creates obvious places to insert a tool. The cost is extra model calls, so the graph should call a model only when it needs language and keep the control decisions in ordinary code. That is the difference between a demo that happens to call tools and a workflow you can operate.

title: Why the control flow is a graph
text: A graph makes the allowed transitions visible. From the planner the crew may research, analyze, or write. From the critic it may revise or hand the draft to a person. There is no edge that lets the writer publish on its own. A conditional edge is a function from state to the next node name, so the route can be unit tested without a model. Loops are legal, which is why every loop here stores a counter in state and reads a max chosen before the run starts. When the counter is exhausted the edge leaves the loop even if a model asked for another turn.

title: A guardrail for cited answers
text: A guardrail sits after drafting and checks that every non-obvious claim has a citation back to a retrieved passage. It is deliberately not another open-ended model call. The check looks for required sections, resolves each citation id against the source list, and rejects ids that were quarantined. A score is useful in the trace, but a hard failure is what routes the draft back to the writer. The model may explain the failure in a sentence or two. It does not get to mark its own homework as passing.

title: Retrieved text is data, not instructions
text: Pages in a corpus can contain instructions aimed at the model. Those lines were not typed by the user and they do not outrank the task. The researcher scans each hit for injection phrases and for obvious personal data such as an email address. One matching line quarantines the whole chunk. The id stays in the trace so the run is auditable, and the body is withheld from the writer. The critic then fails the draft if a quarantined id is cited or if a known payload phrase leaks into the prose. This is a tested filter, not a claim that prompt injection is a solved problem.

title: Human approval is a node, not a comment
text: Human-in-the-loop means the graph pauses on a checkpoint and waits for a decision. The pause is an interrupt inside the human review node. The checkpointer stores the thread state under a thread id, so a later request can resume that node with approve or revise. Auto-approve exists for tests and batch evaluation so those runs do not wait on a person. It is a flag in state, not a missing node. A reviewer who asks for another revision is routed back to the writer only while the revision counter is still under its cap.

title: Short-term state and long-term vector memory
text: Short-term state is the working set for a single run: the plan, the sources, the draft, the critique, and the counters. It lives in the graph state and, when a checkpointer is attached, in the thread checkpoint. Long-term vector memory is a different store. After an approved brief passes the guardrail, a summary is embedded and written to disk. A later run can recall that summary while planning. Unapproved drafts are not written there, so a rejected brief does not become evidence for the next question.

title: How to evaluate a small research crew
text: Evaluation of a RAG assistant should check retrieval and the final answer separately, because a single automatic score cannot prove the system is safe to show users. A useful small task set looks for signs you can compute: required sections, valid citations, forbidden leaks, and a metric that had to come from a tool. Run that set on the offline backend in CI so a broken route fails the build. Keep a second, optional run against a real model before a live demo. Publish the numbers you measured and the command that reproduces them.

title: Citation habit for generated briefs
text: A citation is a marker that points at a source id the retriever returned, written next to the sentence it supports. Orphan markers, markers that point at quarantined ids, and a findings list with no markers are failures. The sources section repeats the same ids with titles so a reader can see the map. Limitations belong in the brief even when the run went well, because the corpus is small, the embedder is a hash, and a teaching metric is not a benchmark. Leaving that section out is enough to send the draft back for revision.

title: Traces, tokens, and estimated cost
text: Every node records a span with the node name, wall-clock latency, a one-line detail, and, when a model was called, the token counts. The offline backend estimates tokens from text length and prices them at zero. An OpenAI-compatible backend reads the usage object on the response and applies a small price table. The sum is an estimate for comparing runs, not an invoice. Structured logs carry the same fields, which is enough to see that a critique loop ran once more than you expected without storing every prompt.
